title: Chomsky Hierarchy
body:
The ladder itself. Four classes of [[Languages]], nested strictly inside one another, each
one defined three ways at once: by what shape of grammar rule generates it, by what machine
recognises it, and by what memory that machine gets. Chomsky's original point was linguistic
(which of these can describe a natural language), and it turned out to be the organising
table for [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].

$$\text{regular} \subset \text{context-free} \subset \text{context-sensitive} \subset \text{recursively enumerable}$$

## The table

| Type | Class | Grammar rules look like | Machine | Memory it gets |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | [[Regular Languages\|regular]] | $A \to aB$ or $A \to a$ (one variable, always on the same side) | [[Finite Automata]] | the current state, nothing else |
| 2 | context-free | $A \to \gamma$ (one variable on the left, anything on the right) | [[Pushdown Automata]] | a [[Stack]] |
| 1 | context-sensitive | $\alpha A \beta \to \alpha \gamma \beta$ (rules may look at the neighbours) | linear bounded automaton | tape limited to the input length |
| 0 | recursively enumerable | $\alpha \to \beta$, no restriction | [[Turing Machine]] | unbounded tape |

Read it as one idea: **restricting the grammar and restricting the memory are the same
restriction seen from two ends.** Type 3 rules cannot remember anything about what has
already been generated, and a finite automaton cannot remember anything about what it has
already read. Loosen one side and the other loosens with it.

The numbering is backwards from the containment, which trips people up: type 3 is the
smallest class, type 0 the largest.

## Each containment is strict

The nesting is not just "as far as anyone knows". At every level there is a witness
language the level below provably cannot manage:

| Boundary | Witness | Why the level below fails |
|---|---|---|
| regular ⊂ context-free | $\{a^n b^n\}$ | needs an unbounded count; the [[Pumping Lemma]] proves no [[DFA]] has one |
| context-free ⊂ context-sensitive | $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ | a [[Stack]] can match one pair, not two at once (pumping lemma for CFLs) |
| context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable | the halting language $A_{TM}$ | recognisable but not decidable, see [[Undecidability]] |

And the ladder does not stop at type 0: the languages that are not even recursively
enumerable sit outside it entirely (the *complement* of the halting language is the standard
example). There are uncountably many languages and only countably many machines, so almost
every language is off the chart.

## The decidable level that is missing

The hierarchy has a rung the classical four skip. Between context-sensitive and recursively
enumerable sit the **decidable** (recursive) languages: a machine that halts on every input,
accepting or rejecting. Recursively enumerable only promises it halts on the strings that
are *in* the language. That distinction is the whole of [[Undecidability]], and it is worth
penciling in as a fifth row.

## Why it is worth memorising

- It tells you which tool a problem wants. Matching a token pattern is regular, so
  [[Regular Expressions]] are enough. Matching nested brackets is context-free, so a regex
  cannot do it and you need a parser. This is the practical payoff.
- It explains the shape of a compiler: lexer (regular) then parser (context-free), two
  stages because they sit on two rungs.
- Natural language is the original question, and the answer is roughly "context-free is
  close but not enough", which is why the hierarchy exists at all.

## Core Facts to Know

- Four classes, type 3 (smallest) to type 0 (largest), nested strictly.
- regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable.
- Grammar restriction and machine memory are two views of the same restriction.
- Regular = [[Finite Automata]]; context-free = [[Pushdown Automata]]; context-sensitive =
  linear bounded automaton; recursively enumerable = [[Turing Machine]].
- $\{a^n b^n\}$ separates regular from context-free; $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ separates context-free
  from context-sensitive.
- The decidable languages are a rung the four types leave unnamed, between types 1 and 0.
- Some languages are outside type 0 entirely, by a counting argument.
